entities.name: Globe Theatre
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Globe Theatre was the playhouse built in 1599 in Southwark, London by the acting company to which William Shakespeare belonged — the Lord Chamberlain's Men, later the King's Men. The timber-framed, open-air theater constructed with timbers from the dismantled Theatre in Shoreditch hosted the first performances of Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth, and many of Shakespeare's greatest works, making it the most historically important theater in the English-speaking world.

The Globe was a circular, three-story structure accommodating approximately 3,000 spectators: wealthy patrons in covered galleries surrounding an open-air pit where 'groundlings' stood for a penny. The thrust stage extended into the yard, surrounded by spectators on three sides, creating the intimate relationship between actor and audience that characterizes Shakespearean performance. The thatched roof caught fire during a 1613 performance of Henry VIII and burned to the ground; a second Globe (with a tiled roof) operated until 1644, when Puritan authorities closed London's theaters.

The Globe Theatre was rebuilt in 1997 as 'Shakespeare's Globe,' 230 meters from the original site on the Bankside, using historical construction methods: green oak, lime plaster, and Norfolk water reed thatch (the only new thatched roof permitted in London since 1666). The reconstructed theater performs Shakespeare under original conditions — no microphones, no artificial lighting during day performances. Sam Wanamaker, the American actor who championed the reconstruction, died in 1993 before seeing it completed.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Globe Theatre hosted the first performances of Shakespeare's greatest works and defined the theatrical conventions of the English Renaissance, making it the single most historically significant theater in the English language.
